title: Economic development strategy and transit corridor monitoring
subtitle: Speedsville Road transfer, U-Pass update, Ion phase 2 schedule, tariffs direction and a Cambridge water concern.
overview: The Sustainability, Infrastructure, and Development Committee heard two major reports for information. The first was the draft 2025 Waterloo Region Economic Development Strategy, built around talent, land readiness, scaling innovation, strategic sector support and quality of life. Staff plan to return to Regional Council in spring for final approval. The second was the Central Transit Corridor monitoring report, which staff said shows the Ion corridor changing as expected, with population, ridership and building activity growing.

The committee recommended that Council begin the process of transferring Speedsville Road, between Regional Roads 38 and 39, from the City of Cambridge to the Region {{vote:m2}}. The change would put the road under Regional ownership and bring its traffic rules into the Region's by-laws. It also approved the consent agenda, which included receiving the 2025 Laurier U-Pass update {{vote:m1}}.

Committee members also gave staff direction, without a separate motion, to report back on how tariffs could affect local businesses and on residential tenure in the transit corridor. Staff said Ion phase 2 public engagement begins in May, with a costed business case expected in the fourth quarter. A councillor also raised a water-taking concern near Cambridge. The committee's next meeting is February 11.

decisions.item: Speedsville Road transfer to the Region
decisions.detail: The committee recommended starting the process to transfer Speedsville Road between Regional Roads 38 and 39 from Cambridge to the Region, including public notice and amendments to the road consolidation and traffic and parking by-laws.
The committee received for information and approved the consent agenda, which included the 2025 Laurier U-Pass program update {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Councillors asked how the strategy would help with shovel-ready employment land, especially in the townships where little land is available. Staff pointed to a separate shovel-ready strategy due back in a couple of months, covering funding, financing and public-private partnerships. One councillor noted that large areas had already been set aside for industrial and business use.

On talent, staff said student surveys showed many graduates plan to leave the region, partly because they do not know what jobs exist. Staff said younger people also value transit, access to a family doctor and affordability. Members asked about skills training beyond universities, and staff cited apprenticeships and trades.

Members asked about AI, food and agriculture, and possible US tariffs. Staff said the strategy treats AI mainly through helping start-ups scale up and agreed to consider the food strategy in more detail. Staff also said they would monitor how tariffs affect local firms. One councillor asked for a report back on this.

On the transit corridor, councillors welcomed the growth but noted little affordable housing has been built there. Staff pointed to land acquisition for phase 2 and said cities are lowering parking requirements. A township councillor said intensification benefits the cities more than the townships.

On Ion phase 2, one councillor was disappointed that the business case is again weighing options, including bus rapid transit. Staff said comparing options is a required step and that a transfer would be a factor in the analysis. The chair asked members to keep questions to the monitoring report.
